title: What Vague Words Cost Your Team
summary: Words like "cleaner" or "soon" feel harmless in a meeting and turn into rework later. Where the cost of vague language lands, and the simple habits that keep it small.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
In a design review someone says, "Let's make the checkout cleaner." Everyone nods. Who wants a messy checkout? Two weeks later the designer has tightened the spacing, the engineer has merged two steps into one, and the product owner is still waiting for the promo-code field to disappear. Three people, three versions of "cleaner," and a sprint of work that now needs a second pass.

Vague words feel free when you say them. The bill shows up later, and someone else usually pays it. This post looks at where that cost lands and at a few habits that keep it small.

Where the cost lands

Vague language feels polite. It leaves room, skips the awkward moment and lets the meeting end on time. Early in a project that's often fine, since not every half-formed idea needs a hard definition. Trouble starts when a vague sentence becomes the spec people build from.

The most visible cost is rework. A feature is technically done but isn't what someone pictured. A doc is complete but answers the wrong question. A design review spends thirty minutes arguing taste because nobody named the user behavior the change was supposed to protect. Nobody was careless. The target was never sharp enough to aim at.

The less visible cost is stress that flows downhill. In The Curse of Knowledge, Chip and Dan Heath point to strategy lines like "Achieving customer delight!" and "Unlocking shareholder value!" To the executives who wrote them, each phrase sits on years of concrete knowledge. To people on the front line, who don't have that context, the same words are opaque. Product teams do this all the time. "Make it premium" or "make it enterprise-ready" sounds like direction, but someone still has to turn it into decisions: which edge case matters, which metric should move, which user should notice. If nobody does that translation out loud, it lands on the people furthest from the original intent.

Engineers solved this once already

Spec writers hit the same problem long ago. When an internet standard says a client "should" retry, does it have to? RFC 2119, published in 1997, settled it by defining a handful of words. MUST means an absolute requirement. SHOULD means there may be valid reasons to skip it in particular circumstances, as long as you understand the full implications first. Twenty years later, RFC 8174 tightened it further: the words only carry those meanings when written in capitals. The original RFC also says these words "must be used with care and sparingly," which is good advice for any team vocabulary.

Your team doesn't need an RFC. It needs the same move: when a word is about to carry real weight, agree on what it means before anyone builds on it.

Ask for an example

The fastest way to sharpen a vague word is to ask for an example. "Cleaner" becomes "a returning customer can pay in two taps instead of four." Matt Wynne's Example Mapping turns this into a habit. A small group writes the story on a yellow card, the rules on blue cards, concrete examples on green cards and open questions on red cards. A well-understood, well-sized story takes about 25 minutes. A pile of red cards means the team isn't ready to build yet, and that's a cheap thing to learn on day one.

In any meeting, a few questions do the same job:

  • What does "cleaner" mean here? Can you show me one before-and-after?
  • What should stay exactly as it is?
  • How will we know we're done?
  • Which trade-off are we accepting?

These questions slow the room down for five minutes. In exchange, nobody walks out holding a private version of the plan. If you write tickets, the same thinking goes into good acceptance criteria.

The version we all do

There's a personal version too. We keep a concern vague because naming it would make us responsible for it. "This feels a bit off" instead of "this breaks when two people edit the same record." "Soon" instead of a date. "We need more alignment" when what we mean is that nobody has made the decision yet. Each one keeps the moment comfortable and borrows against trust later.

A useful test: could someone who wasn't in the meeting act on this sentence? If not, it's still a thought. That's fine, as long as everyone knows it's a thought. Problems start when thoughts get treated as commitments and commitments get written like moods.

Not every conversation has to sound like a contract. Exploring needs room for half-ideas and metaphors. The skill is spotting the moment when exploring has to turn into something with edges, usually right before the work starts. Being clear at that point is often the kinder move, because the disagreement happens while changing course is still cheap.

Try this week

  • Pick one word your team uses as if everyone agrees on it ("done," "stable," "MVP") and ask three people what it means.
  • In your next review, ask for one before-and-after example before anyone debates the design.
  • Swap one "soon" in a status update for a date, or for "I'll know by Thursday."
  • Run a 25-minute Example Mapping session on the next fuzzy story.

faqs.q: Why is vague communication costly for teams?
faqs.a: Because each person fills in the gaps differently, and the mismatch only shows up once work is done. The result is rework, long debates about taste, and pressure on the people who had to guess what a leader meant.

faqs.q: How do you turn a vague request into something actionable?
faqs.a: Ask for a concrete example, ideally a before-and-after. Then ask what should stay unchanged, how you will know you are done and which trade-off you are accepting.

A short workshop created by Matt Wynne. A small group writes a user story on a yellow card, rules on blue cards, examples on green cards and open questions on red cards. A well-sized story takes about 25 minutes.

faqs.q: What does RFC 2119 have to do with team communication?
faqs.a: RFC 2119 defined words like MUST and SHOULD so internet specs mean the same thing to every reader. Teams can borrow the idea: agree on what loaded words such as "done" or "stable" mean before building on them.
